newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's Mandela says ANC spies must be exposed.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's Mandela says ANC spies must be exposed.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela said on Monday that people in his ruling African National Congress (ANC) who served as informents for the apartheid government had to be exposed.

Allegations surfaced recently during enquiries by Archbishop Desmond Tutu's truth commission that up to five ANC cabinet ministers spied on their own colleagues for the white regime during the war over apartheid.

"We are trying to establish a transparent society...Why should any particular individual be protected?" Mandela told reporters after arriving back in South Africa from a 10-day visit to southeast Asia.
"I am in favour of exposure of all people who served the apartheid regime and whose actions may have led to massacres of innocent people."

The statutory Truth and Reconciliation Commission's (TRC) amnesty committee initially ruled that spies identified during applications for immunity from prosecution for human rights crimes would not be publicly named.
But Tutu said last week it would be necessary to name the people implicated after giving them 21 days advance notice in order to halt the spread of lies and innuendo.
The ANC met in Johannesburg on Monday to discuss revealing the names of alleged apartheid-era informers in its ranks.
"The ANC has always insisted on full disclosure as part of the process of reconciliation," it said in a statement after the meeting.

But it warned: "We have also learnt that part of the strategy of the apartheid regime's security and intelligence establishment was to destabilise and paralyse the ANC and its allies through rumour-mongering and casting aspersions on the loyalty of some leaders."
The outcome will be a test for the ANC, which has promoted open government and transparency in politics since it swept to power in the country's first all-race elections in 1994.
Roelof du Plessis, a lawyer representing five apartheid agents seeking amnesty, told the TRC there were high-profile people in government who were informers.
Joe Mamasela, who has confessed to several political murders, has said five ANC cabinet ministers had once worked for the apartheid police.
Mandela and deputy president Thabo Mbeki have come out in favour of naming the alleged informers, with Mandela saying anyone whose actions led to deaths would be fired from the cabinet.

Mandela said during his four-nation tour of southeast Asia last week that intelligence reports showed there were "high profile people, not necessarily in cabinet," who had informed on their colleagues in the past.

Scores of police and soldiers who served the white governments of the past have given testimony to Tutu's commission or the amnesty committee about torture, kidnapping and assassination aimed at the ANC.
But ANC members accused of human rights abuses in the movement's training camps have yet to appear before the TRC.
"We have no interest in protecting informers," Matthews Phosa, the ANC's legal adviser and now premier of Mpumalanga province told state radio on Monday.
The TRC, set up to heal apartheid's wounds, can grant indemnity from prosecution to those who confess to crimes or human rights abuses committed on either side of the race war.
